lxc_2203d6fff3071040.text: Some physicists have explored the possibility that black holes could create new universes.

lxc_e825d88134b8977e.text: Physicist Lee Smolin took this idea further: perhaps universes reproduce, slightly change, and go through something similar to natural selection.

lxc_1626a748a41b097c.text: Could Black Holes Be the Children of Other Universes?

lxc_638e84ef5d124c99.text: Some physicists have explored the possibility that black holes could create new universes.

lxc_46f8b293705aa985.text: Physicist Lee Smolin took this idea further: perhaps universes reproduce, slightly change, and go through something similar to natural selection.

lxc_ee2e23f27061c8cb.text: This is a serious scientific hypothesis, but it has not been proven.

lxc_3c9b69b3a589e5de.text: We normally imagine the Big Bang as the absolute beginning.

lxc_1f57fdba9f22a0d7.text: About 13.8 billion years ago, our observable universe was extremely hot and dense.

lxc_3efd46d2ddae94b0.text: Space expanded, matter formed, stars appeared, planets developed, and eventually life became possible.

lxc_ce6d7434da38b0b2.text: But this leaves one enormous question: Why did the Big Bang happen at all?

lxc_f7b388e8d71fc462.text: And another: Was it truly the beginning, or did something exist before it?

lxc_e21df555471263ee.text: One strange possibility is that our universe was born inside something else.

lxc_eb06e474edf9699d.text: Imagine a black hole existing in an older universe.

lxc_baebcabdb177d9a9.text: From the outside, matter falls into the black hole and seems to disappear behind the event horizon.

lxc_3a0b51bb07cca628.text: But perhaps the story does not end there.

lxc_32e292e7cb21de94.text: Some speculative theories of quantum gravity suggest that the extreme collapse inside a black hole might not continue forever into an infinitely dense singularity.

lxc_4c9e655c7cf90bb0.text: That bounce might create a new expanding region of spacetime.

lxc_2404972b31c2225f.text: From inside that new region, the event might look surprisingly similar to a Big Bang.

lxc_37cc5834cc5b6ac3.text: This leads to the first crazy possibility: A black hole in one universe could become the beginning of another universe.

lxc_b35f4b3b3f66d387.text: A black hole forms when enough matter becomes concentrated in a small region.

lxc_07ed2f927b65ca3d.text: Its gravity becomes so strong that beyond the event horizon, even light cannot escape.

lxc_dcba5bab179be0c5.text: According to classical general relativity, matter falling deep inside eventually approaches a singularity—a region where the equations predict extreme curvature and our normal description of spacetime breaks down.

lxc_11aa6ee3232bb6ea.text: But physicists do not usually interpret this as proof that nature literally contains an infinitely dense point.

lxc_4bffe95731eb13b6.text: It may instead mean: Our current theory has reached its limit.

lxc_4efd9f42ce39fb6f.text: General relativity describes gravity extremely well.

lxc_2b478c76d0017ecd.text: Quantum mechanics describes very small systems extremely well.

lxc_39dcf93ccf378983.text: Inside a black hole, however, we need to understand both extreme gravity and quantum physics at the same time.

lxc_a422d4c70c799638.text: We still do not have a complete theory of quantum gravity.

lxc_ac517010c9711102.text: Because of this, we do not know with confidence what happens at the deepest interior of a black hole.

lxc_617d451c6b144c7b.text: And that uncertainty leaves room for ideas such as a bounce or a baby universe.

lxc_4214f1d194fda02c.text: Now imagine falling toward a black hole.

lxc_0269e6ab49225652.text: From the perspective of someone far away, you cross the event horizon and can never communicate back.

lxc_ce2d7e35d7415311.text: But suppose the interior geometry continues into a new expanding region.

lxc_1750067b6aad2d8c.text: That new region might become separated from the original universe.

lxc_d84976eb2b0c09b5.text: People in the parent universe would simply see: a black hole.

lxc_226e728c0d4f2888.text: But hypothetical observers inside the new region might see: an expanding universe.

lxc_f20a3dacdaa7d09d.text: This is why these hypothetical regions are sometimes called baby universes.

lxc_8ac60e12d8ec126d.text: The parent and child might remain connected in a mathematical description of spacetime, or the child universe might effectively “pinch off” and become causally separate.

lxc_23de26f70727716e.text: If it became fully separate, inhabitants of the child universe might have no way of discovering their parent directly.

lxc_c650450b29de5664.text: This produces an extraordinary possibility: Every black hole we see might hide an enormous expanding universe on the other side.

lxc_1a1fde1b3d2a6e71.text: A small object from our perspective could therefore contain an entire cosmos from another perspective.

lxc_418137b23c5a4c7f.text: The idea becomes much stranger with physicist Lee Smolin.

lxc_a7c7d601eedf51e3.text: Smolin asked: If black holes create new universes, what happens if the new universes are slightly different from their parents?

lxc_7c2f319a65ec0949.text: Suppose a universe has physical constants.

lxc_f751f1bbb5cb43b5.text:
These constants control things such as:

• particle masses

• forces

• nuclear reactions

• gravity

• star formation

Now imagine that when a black hole produces a child universe, these values change slightly.

lxc_608ca08f8a666f36.text: The child therefore resembles the parent but is not exactly identical.

lxc_de3baccd0712d917.text: This gives us something surprisingly similar to biological reproduction.

lxc_9f8261e83df5fdf0.text:
Biology

Parent organism → child → slightly different genes

Cosmology

Parent universe → black hole → child universe → slightly different physical constants

Once reproduction and variation exist, another possibility appears: selection.

lxc_2e3a3c940ef9cae6.text: Some organisms have traits that help them reproduce.

lxc_b57c4f17e29ebb24.text: Their traits therefore become more common in future generations.

lxc_f0ac71d8a01e2f45.text: Smolin asked whether something similar could happen to universes.

lxc_ed41a3a9d6c76cda.text:
Universe A

Its physical laws produce very few stars.

lxc_5aaf9570a6282107.text: Very few stars means very few black holes.

lxc_790ec78178cf08ea.text:
It produces: 10 child universes

Universe B

Its physical laws are excellent for creating large stars.

lxc_6046af22af7e85ac.text: Many large stars eventually collapse into black holes.

lxc_37e0c5d2c8163b7f.text:
It produces: 1,000,000 child universes

If the child universes inherit approximately similar physical laws, then after many generations, universes like B become much more common.

lxc_9c939a6dfc7befdf.text: Not because they are trying to survive.

lxc_0aad3c6631dca2c8.text: Simply because: Universes that make more black holes make more universes.

lxc_c65394a667869499.text: Smolin called this idea Cosmological Natural Selection.

lxc_dc9799f180c9fbd0.text: Normally we ask: “Why do the laws of physics have these particular values?”

lxc_49d77367b2d9ce5f.text: For example, why does gravity have its exact strength?

lxc_bcabdb49d86cae51.text: Why do particles have their particular masses?

lxc_62631c938eb0f3f8.text: Why do nuclear reactions work in a way that allows stars to exist?

lxc_7772514cca9529ee.text: Usually these values are treated as basic facts of our universe.

lxc_eba157cd1bc57d98.text: Smolin's hypothesis suggests a radically different possibility: Perhaps these values have a history.

lxc_417ac0bb773cff87.text: They may be similar to biological traits.

lxc_6d344a70395fac7a.text: Imagine changing one physical constant slightly.

lxc_66abe0a3ac5755bf.text: Another set of constants may produce enormous numbers of long-lived stars and black holes.

lxc_db9da86efe05f666.text: After many cosmic generations, the population of universes could become concentrated around laws that are especially good at producing black holes.

lxc_665706537b1288c1.text: In this picture, the laws of nature that look “special” may not have been chosen.

lxc_89f6800ef333090b.text: That is an enormous conceptual change.

lxc_1f66ccd3889aa434.text: Instead of asking: “Who designed these constants?”

lxc_e076af831d3e42d7.text: we could ask: “Did these constants evolve?”

lxc_c0ac860955844c02.text:
Our universe happens to have laws that allow:

• stable stars

• heavy chemical elements

• carbon

• planets

• complex chemistry

• life

This is sometimes called the fine-tuning problem.

lxc_ba0c46a52121971a.text: Why does the universe seem so suitable for complexity?

lxc_5d3d5fdecf3f38d7.text: One answer is the anthropic principle: We observe a universe compatible with life because otherwise we would not exist to observe it.

lxc_6a2d9cb689e48740.text: But cosmological natural selection gives a different possibility.

lxc_882190baca033270.text: Perhaps the universe was not selected for life.

lxc_73905cbe1121b0c5.text: Perhaps it was selected for black holes.

lxc_1f22260e006cb4dc.text: Life might simply be a side effect.

lxc_5fb8e3ff99fd22a5.text:
The conditions that help create black holes also require complex astrophysics: stars → nuclear fusion → heavy elements → supernovae → black holes

Those same stars also create the carbon, oxygen, iron, and other elements needed for planets and life.

lxc_eddfc974d086fb67.text: So perhaps: The universe was not “designed” for us at all.

lxc_9bea55e911e3f8ac.text: We may simply benefit from physical conditions that were good at producing stars and black holes.

lxc_30cb047788418b10.text: Life could be an accidental passenger inside a universe optimized for something completely different.

lxc_3efbbed403d7523f.text: If this process happened repeatedly, reality might contain a gigantic family tree of universes.

lxc_d7826b17200923aa.text:
Imagine:

Universe 1 ↓ 1,000 black holes ↓ 1,000 child universes ↓ each produces thousands of black holes ↓ millions of grandchildren universes

After enough generations, the number could become enormous.

lxc_1ff94743d2989333.text: Some branches would die quickly because their physics produces almost no black holes.

lxc_b05efa30208f958c.text: Other branches would reproduce extremely successfully.

lxc_d6ef95321d728efb.text: The multiverse would therefore not be a random collection of universes.

lxc_43e764b85a0d54bd.text:
It could have:

• ancestry

• generations

• inheritance

• variation

• selection

In other words: The multiverse could have a history.

lxc_2e99997e137fd320.text: Just as every human belongs to an enormous biological family tree, our universe might belong to a cosmic family tree stretching through realities we can never directly observe.

lxc_f51b26f915d64e70.text: This hypothesis also changes the meaning of a black hole.

lxc_231dae0558b2734b.text: They are often described as cosmic graves.

lxc_86da7729fc26f3c9.text:
But under the baby-universe idea, a black hole could simultaneously be: death from one perspective

and: birth from another.

lxc_ea689a03f1315d41.text: A collapsing star in our universe could produce a Big Bang somewhere else.

lxc_57d4a2a0655838ad.text:
This creates a beautiful symmetry:

Star dies → black hole forms → new universe begins → new stars form → new black holes form → more universes begin

Destruction becomes reproduction.

lxc_4b91aa838e8bdf82.text: The objects we call the “dead ends” of spacetime could actually be its reproductive organs.

lxc_3b9d7af0b3c95e7b.text: That is perhaps the wildest part of the idea.

lxc_a21155099fb0ac4c.text: If black holes in our universe create baby universes, perhaps our universe is also a baby universe.

lxc_7d2c8ae0ee9e92e9.text: Then somewhere in a parent cosmos, billions of years—or perhaps a completely different kind of time—ago, a star or other enormous structure may have collapsed.

lxc_9893d242ef2edeb6.text: From the parent's perspective: matter disappeared behind an event horizon.

lxc_68013b151f67b36f.text: From our perspective: spacetime began expanding.

lxc_442f4acedd172beb.text: Our Big Bang could therefore be the inside view of something that looked like a black hole from outside.

lxc_63ea120508281260.text: If true, asking: “What happened before the Big Bang?”

lxc_1f3e2915a3c07c49.text: might be similar to asking: “What happened in the parent universe?”

lxc_93132624c2bc1b85.text: But there is a serious difficulty.

lxc_9f808a77f04c8552.text: The causal structure of a black hole may prevent information from the parent universe from reaching us.

lxc_ed3254edde22a144.text: We might literally be unable to look backward beyond our own cosmic birth.

lxc_50eb52ad4d6edbb9.text: This is where we must separate fascinating physics from established physics.

lxc_f83dc7d4991fdcd6.text: We have strong astronomical evidence for them, including gravitational-wave detections and images of black-hole environments.

lxc_8b33ae548f4f8d61.text: But we do not know that black holes create universes.

lxc_f641fd061f1f3f36.text: That requires physics beyond our currently confirmed understanding of black-hole interiors.

lxc_98e73fd07bbb872f.text: Smolin tried to make his theory scientifically useful by proposing a prediction.

lxc_031be2eae89537b3.text: If universes have evolved to maximize black-hole production, then the physical constants in our universe should be close to values that produce unusually many black holes.

lxc_6b4daef6df80d286.text: If scientists could change one constant slightly in a theoretical model and reliably produce more black holes, that could challenge the hypothesis.

lxc_a0526575dfec1751.text: This makes the proposal more interesting than simply saying: “Maybe other universes exist.”

lxc_76e9e7f14e9c1fc3.text: It tries to connect the idea to things we can calculate about our universe.

lxc_7f72d5e6198462b8.text: However, scientists continue to debate whether these tests are strong enough and whether the biological natural-selection analogy really works.

lxc_6f63b79e477e949c.text: Cosmological natural selection is not the standard accepted explanation of our universe.

lxc_8b80f2e872aae7ba.text: But the broader questions behind it remain active in theoretical physics.

lxc_340b141fbe0536c2.text:
Researchers continue to study:

• black-hole interiors

• quantum gravity

• singularity removal

• cosmological bounces

• wormholes

• baby universes

Even in 2026, theoretical papers continue exploring mathematical models where baby universes can emerge from black-hole interiors or early-universe processes.

lxc_ad71d99e0bb95b4e.text: This does not mean Smolin's full theory has been confirmed.

lxc_f8a7ee1291170c8a.text:
It means the deeper question—

Can one region of spacetime produce another expanding universe?

lxc_aeeaf6830882dbb0.text: The most powerful part of this hypothesis may not even be the black holes.

lxc_9222063a0911be0c.text: It is the idea that we might be thinking about the laws of nature incorrectly.

lxc_e356d8004195b897.text:
We usually imagine: laws first → universe follows laws

But cosmological natural selection suggests: universes reproduce → laws vary → some laws reproduce more successfully

Now the laws themselves become part of history.

lxc_3a5e61ebc3933093.text: This is similar to what Darwin did to biology.

lxc_0095664e8dd61f21.text: A tiger was simply a tiger.

lxc_dc32aa9b801f69d5.text: After Darwin, a tiger became the current result of a historical process.

lxc_64f59c6e7dcea294.text: Smolin asks whether we could make the same conceptual change in physics.

lxc_93c06fcc4691fc43.text: Perhaps an electron's mass or gravity's strength is not simply: “the number nature chose.”

lxc_7c553257a6fbd59d.text: Perhaps it is: the surviving result of a cosmic evolutionary history.

lxc_d2e3a4b64b81760f.text: Whether this is true or not, that question completely changes how we think about the universe.
